text.text: The newsroom in one place. Stories is the budget from pitch to published, with the publish slot, fact check and art; Events to cover lists the meetings and hearings someone must attend; Sources is the contact book; Interviews tracks who has been reached; Corrections keeps the record honest. pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of the newsroom in this workspace. Share it with every editor, reporter and photographer.
: the budget. Each story's desk, format, reporter, editor, filing deadline, publish time and slot, fact check, art, pageviews and open corrections.
: public meetings, hearings, press conferences and games, with who is going.
: everyone who must be reached for a story, linked to the source, with how they may be quoted.
: the contact book by beat, with agreed terms and when you last spoke.
: every reported error, its fix-by date and outcome.
Morning meeting: today's slots, new pitches, tonight's events.
Reporters report and file by their deadline.
Evening: tonight's meeting stories filed; tomorrow's newsletter set.
Every morning: publish schedule for today, overdue filings, open corrections
Every week: events for the next seven days assigned; sources not called in a month
Every month: pageviews by desk, corrections patterns
Every quarter: beats and the source book reviewed
The managing editor owns the budget and corrections. Editors own their desks' stories from assignment to publish. Reporters own their stories, sources and interviews. Photographers own art requests.

We name sources whenever we can, we give people we write about a real chance to respond, and we never publish a number we cannot show where it came from. When in doubt, the editor decides, and the decision is written in the story's notes.
Sources' phone numbers and notes are confidential. A source granted background terms is never named in the workspace text that others can see beyond the newsroom.
Rename desks, slots and formats to your newsroom and delete the sample rows once your own are in. Edit any cell in place and drag cards between columns.
The desk at a glance. Charts read the live tables.

text.text: Every story moves through the same stages, and the budget always shows where each one is. If it is not on the budget, it is not happening.
Anyone can pitch. A pitch is two sentences: what is new, and why readers in this county should care. Add it to
with the desk and format. Editors decide at the morning meeting: assign it or kill it with a reason.
The editor sets the reporter, the filing deadline and the length.
The reporter lists who must be reached in
. Every story that criticizes someone gives them a fair chance to respond, with a deadline you would accept yourself.
Documents beat memory: get the budget, the minutes, the inspection report.
The editor reads for fairness, clarity and holes first, then line by line.
: every name, title, number, date and quote is checked against notes or documents. Mark it Done only when every fact has been checked.
: a photo, a chart or a map. Mark what is needed early; photographers book up.
: the morning newsletter, midday, evening, the weekend or the weekly print edition.
The editor gives the final read and moves it to
When it is live, set it to
Some stories do not hold up. Kill them honestly, write why in a line, and thank the people who gave their time.
Today's slots: what is ready, what is late
Tonight's meetings and who is going

The school board budget story is reporting, due tonight. The reporter has the board chair on the record and is waiting on the finance chief. At 4 pm the editor sets it for the evening web slot with a photo needed. The finance chief calls back at 5; the story is edited, fact-checked and live at 9.
Readers forgive mistakes. They do not forgive hiding them. A quick, plain correction is part of the job and protects everything else you publish.
, linked to the story, with the kind of error and a
date. Same day for anything serious.
The editor of the story checks it against notes and documents.
If it is wrong, it is corrected. Set it to
and explain to the person, kindly, what your reporting showed.
If it is a matter of opinion, consider a letter to the editor, not a correction.

Fix the text, then add a note at the bottom of the story: "An earlier version of this story gave the wrong date for the council vote. It is Tuesday, March 4." Say what was wrong and what is right. Do not quietly change it.
For print, run the correction in the next edition in a consistent place.

A wrong name in a crime story, a wrong number that changes the meaning, or a misquote is serious. The managing editor is told at once, the subject is called, and the story is reviewed for other problems.
Each story counts its open corrections. Once a month, read the list: are the errors names, numbers or dates? Most are fixed by better habits in fact-checking, not by blame.
No correction open past its fix-by date
Every Fixed correction has a note on the story
Patterns shared at the staff meeting

A reader emails that the board chair's first name is misspelled. The editor checks the meeting agenda, confirms the error, fixes the name, adds a correction note, and marks it Fixed within the hour. The reporter adds the correct spelling to the source's record.
Public meetings are where local news starts: budgets, zoning, schools and police. Showing up is the first rule of local reporting, and doing it well takes preparation.
for tomorrow and who is assigned.
Read the agenda and the packet. The story is usually on page 40, not page 1.
Pull past stories on the issues coming up.
Arrive early; sign in if required; sit where you can see faces
Note the time of each vote and the count, by name
Get public commenters' names spelled and their neighborhood
Catch officials after the meeting for the quote the meeting did not give
If the vote matters tonight, file a short version within an hour for the evening web slot. Write the longer story for the morning.
Lead with what was decided and what it means for residents, not with the order of the agenda.
time, if it is not already there.
with a reason, watch the recording if there is one, and read the minutes. Never write as if you were there.
Court is not a meeting: names and charges must be exact, and a charge is not a conviction. The editor reads every court story before it runs.

The school board budget workshop starts at 7 pm. The reporter has read the packet and spotted a proposal to close a library branch. She files a 300-word story at 9:15 for the evening web slot and a fuller version with the parents' reaction for the morning newsletter.
